Anecdotally, in my experience, all things being equal including casing, primer, powder, powder charge and bullet type, in my rifle I’ve found a significant difference in group sizes at 100yds from a COL difference of 5/100ths of an inch, the longer COL being the more accurate of the two. This was my firsthand experience that jump to the lands played a significant role in my handloads and now causes me to want to bias my loads towards a slightly longer length than the guides suggest but I resist the urge because I want to develop empirical evidence to prove my suspicion and not put the cart before the horse. Once I generate enough data, I may find a reliable trend that will help to build a more confident bullet seating depth starting point for a particular class of bullet in a particular caliber. All this is to say, I’m willing to spend the money and time now that I’ve the strength and motivation to be the old man that has a hoard of 5k of the same goddamn laser loads sitting in storage right next to my old faithful rifle

What originally caused you to start varying the COL? Do you track velocity as well? I don't think it takes too much data. For one batch of bullets. From what I understand, it may be hard to get a general seating depth from batch to batch. The time consuming part is also add in your velocity and the accuracy node. Then make sure you're on the cold side of it so you go through through the node as your barrel and chamber heat up.

Additional plus side to understanding this stuff is you can make 'shitty' barrels shoot accurately. Most recent project is getting a BCA 6.5 grendel shoot sub MOA.

I have a bolt rifle with a “tighter” chamber than my gas gun and wouldn’t chamber some rounds that had been fire formed through the gas gun. Initially, I incorrectly assumed it was a COL issue so I took a batch of previously seated rounds (COL of 2.78”) and seated them down (COL of 2.72”). When I realized my assumption was incorrect and full length resized with a small base die, my rounds began to chamber flawlessly no matter which gun they were fired in, though my gas gun has lower tolerances and therefore can chamber most full length resized brass just as well as fire formed. So I took the batch of 50, half of which had been seated to a shorter size and ran them all through my gas gun as a test of COL on accuracy through my gas gun. The result was over an inch difference in grouping at 100 yards for average mean radius of 5, 5 shot groups for each length. It was an academic approach and my hypothesis was correct for an n=1 but it was good enough for me to believe everything I had read up to that point about relative COL for a particular chambering. Now I find myself muttering YMMV like all the old heads on the reloading forums for damn near every variable imaginable, but that gas gun will shoot sub .5MOA with the right load and you better believe I made a bunch of that round to age along with me and the rifle. If my barrel life gets close to done with my gas rifle, I’ve already shown that same load to shoot 1MOA through my bolt so I’m not worried about that cartridge aging out through two guns
Also, need to get a chrono, as I’m relying on manuals, overpressure signs and accuracy as an indicator of load suitability. I’d like to hear how your Grendel project works out
